**Ian Joseph Somerhalder**[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-Meroney-1) ( _SUM-ər-hawl-dər_; born December 8, 1978) is an American retired actor. He is known for playing Boone Carlyle in ABC's science fiction adventure drama television series _Lost_ (2004–2010) and Damon Salvatore in the CW supernatural teen drama series _The Vampire Diaries_ (2009–2017).
texts.1:
## Early life
Somerhalder was born on December 8, 1978,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-2) in Covington, Louisiana.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-Hello_Mag-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-5) His mother, Edna (née Israel),[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-6) is a massage therapist of Choctaw and Irish descent[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-7) from Mississippi,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-Minnick-8) while his father, Robert Somerhalder Sr., is an independent building contractor[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-knutzen-9) of Cajun descent.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-Meroney-1)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-Chassen-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-Highfill-11) The second of three children, Somerhalder has an elder brother and a younger sister.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-Rickman-12):2[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-Cave-13)
texts.2:
## Early life
Somerhalder graduated from [Saint Paul's School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Paul's_School_(Louisiana) "St. Paul's School (Louisiana)").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-14) He embarked on a modeling career from age 10[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-knutzen-9)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-Cave-13) to 13.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-15) His parents divorced[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-Meroney-1) when he was 14, and he subsequently lived with his mother.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-Rickman-12):3 At age 17, Somerhalder decided to refocus on acting[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-Hello_Mag-4) and began studying with acting teacher William Esper.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-Rickman-12):8[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-16)
texts.3:
## Career
Somerhalder at the 2015 _Wizard World_ Convention
In the summer of 2000, Somerhalder starred in the short-lived WB series _Young Americans_, a spin-off of _[Dawson's Creek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dawson's\_Creek "Dawson's Creek")_. He played Hamilton Fleming, the son of the dean of a prestigious boarding school. In 2002, Somerhalder played bisexual character Paul Denton in Roger Avary's adaptation of Bret Easton Ellis' novel, _The Rules of Attraction_, alongside James Van Der Beek, Shannyn Sossamon, and Jessica Biel.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-17)
In 2004, Somerhalder scored his breakthrough role when he played Boone Carlyle in _Lost_. Despite his character's death in the twentieth episode of the first season, he returned to the role of Boone for seven more episodes between 2005 and 2010, including the series finale. He was the first major character to die.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-Malcom-18) Following his departure from the show, ABC signed him to another one-year contract.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-19) In 2005, he stated that being a part of _Lost_ was "the greatest experience" of "the greatest year of his life".[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-Williamson-21)
texts.4:
## Career
In 2009, Somerhalder appeared in the movie _The Tournament_ where he played the role of an assassin participating in a lethal competition with other assassins. He appears in the coffee table book _About Face_ by celebrity photographer John Russo.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-23) Also in 2009, Somerhalder began playing the role of Vampire Damon Salvatore as a series regular in The CW television drama series _The Vampire Diaries_. The series premiere attracted The CW's highest premiere ratings of any season premiere since the network began in 2006. The series has continued to be the highest-rated series on its channel with both his performance and the show receiving a positive response from critics. He began directing _The Vampire Diaries_ in its third season and produced the series at the start of season 8. He received several Teen Choice Awards and a [People's Choice Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Choice_Award "People's Choice Award") for his participation on the series.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-24)
Somerhalder acted in the short subject _Time Framed_ (2013).[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-25) He played Dr. Luther Swann as a series regular in the Netflixscience fictionhorror series _V Wars_, which ran from 2019 to 2020.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-26)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-28)
texts.5:
## Career
In 2020, Somerhalder shot footage for and served as an executive producer on the film _Kiss the Ground,_ a documentary centered on regenerative agriculture.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-29) He returned as an executive producer on its follow-up documentary, _Common Ground_, in 2023.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-30)
In a 2024 interview, Somerhalder revealed that he had retired from acting after relocating to a farm outside of Los Angeles, though he would still be involved in producing and environmental activism.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-31)
texts.6:
## Foundations and causes
Paul Wesley, Nina Dobrev and Somerhalder in 2012
Somerhalder was involved in the cleanup after the _Deepwater Horizon_ oil drilling disaster on April 22, 2010. His efforts included cleaning of oiled wildlife and taping public service announcements to let the public know how they could help.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-32) Somerhalder also supports the St. Tammany Humane Society, an organization for animal shelter and welfare. On November 13, 2010, he hosted a Bash on the Bayou charity fundraiser for the Society. During the event, Somerhalder was presented with a donation of $11,100 by _The Vampire Diaries_fandom for his birthday project.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-33)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-34)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-35)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-36)
Together with his _The Vampire Diaries_ co-stars Candice Accola and Michael Trevino, Somerhalder supports the It Gets Better Project, which makes it a goal to prevent suicide among LGBT youth[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-37) associated with The Trevor Project.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-38) For his second campaign, Somerhalder teamed up with _The Vampire Diaries_ co-star Paul Wesley to release a limited edition shirt designed by a fan, with the words "Blood Brothers Since 1864."[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-39) This campaign sold almost 10,000 shirts.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-40)
texts.7:
## Foundations and causes
On December 8, 2010, Somerhalder's 32nd birthday, he launched the "Ian Somerhalder Foundation" which he hopes will educate people on the importance of protecting the environment and animals: "Instead of gifts this year, my birthday wish is that we come together and raise funds to support projects that protect our habitat and nurture our furry friends."[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-41)[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-42) To spread awareness for his foundation, Somerhalder sponsors and often walks in Mardi Paws, a parade and organization held in his hometown of Covington.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-43) He opposes GMO foods and factory farming, and supports ecologistAllan Savory in his crusade to let cows graze in sync with nature to enrich soil, enhance biodiversity, and reverse climate change. In 2011, Somerhalder visited Savory in Africa and announced he was making a documentary about him with the goal of winning him a Nobel Prize.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-isfsavory-44)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-esavory-45)
Somerhalder is also a celebrity campaigner for RYOT, a Los Angeles-based media company known for RYOT.org, its cause-based, take action online news source.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-46)
texts.8:
## Personal life
Somerhalder dated his _Vampire Diaries_ co-star Nina Dobrev from 2010 to 2013.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-47) In 2014, he began dating actress Nikki Reed.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-48) They married on April 26, 2015, in Malibu, California.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-49) They had a daughter in 2017,[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-50)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-51) and a son in 2023.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-52)
While working on _Lost,_ Somerhalder and Maggie Grace adopted a feral cat named Roo which that they found "literally dying" in the jungle, and it later became Grace's "travel buddy."[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-53) Somerhalder stated that being a part of _Lost_ was "the greatest experience" of "the greatest year of his life".[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-54)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-55)
texts.9:
## Personal life
### Brother's Bond Bourbon
Somerhalder has remained close friends with his former _Vampire Diaries_ co-star Paul Wesley, and in 2020, they announced the launch of a straight bourbon whiskey named Brother's Bond Bourbon.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-56)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-57)

### NEED TO KNOW
*   Ian Somerhalder stepped away from Hollywood in August 2019

*   In a new interview, he revealed the "really honest" reason behind his exit, which was a result of _V Wars_' cancellation

*   "I am not here for my career and livelihood to be dictated by someone who has mommy or daddy issues, or they weren't popular in school," he said
Nearly seven years after his exit, Ian Somerhalder is finally revealing the true reason he quit acting.
Somerhalder, 47, departed Hollywood in August 2019 and has since turned his focus to other business ventures with his wife, Nikki Reed, after they moved to a Calif. farm.
He shared the "really honest, kind of controversial" reason that he decided to pivot on the July 9 episode of the _Haley on the Go_ podcast, as he recalled how the cancellation of his Netflix series, _V Wars_, affected him.
"I wanted to do _V Wars_ because it was me, not as a vampire, it was me as a scientist," he said of the series. "[We] shot the show, moved my whole family to Northern Ontario. Worked really hard on this thing for almost a year, and the show that got turned in wasn't even watchable."
"I said to the studio, I don't want to put my name on this. I'll give you the money back — I'll give you millions of dollars. And they were like, 'What? What are you talking about?' "
_Ian Somerhalder in 'V Wars'_
_Credit: Netflix_
Somerhalder claimed he told Netflix that he and his producing partner, James Gibb, needed "creative control of the show" to fix it. "Netflix said, 'Sure. We're not giving you a dollar more.' "
He and Gibb raised more than $6 million to fix the series, Somerhalder said, and filmed "10 or 12 hours of footage in about six days," which landed him "in the hospital" from overworking his body.
texts.1:
### NEED TO KNOW
When the show premiered in December 2019, it was a "hit," Somerhalder said, but it was canceled anyway. Somerhalder alleged, "The execs were fighting, and someone quietly canceled the show. And the powers that be at Netflix were like, 'It's unfortunate. Yes, it shouldn't have happened. We can't go back, because it would set a precedent that would be terrible, so the show is done.' "
"I looked at myself in the mirror, and I said to my wife, I was like, man, I'm 40 years old. I don't want to spend two years of my life doing something, working this hard — one year fully unpaid — for this executive who had issues in high school, so they want to exert power now, [to cancel it]," Somerhalder said. "I am not here for my career and livelihood to be dictated by someone who has mommy or daddy issues, or they weren't popular in school."
"So I pulled the plug. That was it. I walked away," he said. "These executives are bitching at each other, and I'm like, are you kidding me? Done. I'm out."

_Credit: Gregg DeGuire/Getty_
There's a possibility, albeit slim, of Somerhalder making a return to Hollywood. In 2024, he told PEOPLE that acting is "in the rearview mirror," but also shared a more positive update.
"We got the rights back for _V Wars_," he revealed. "But I just don't know how the hell we would ever make a TV show."

He was the first major character to die.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-Malcom-18) Following his departure from the show, ABC signed him to another one-year contract.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-19) In 2005, he stated that being a part of _Lost_ was "the greatest experience" of "the greatest year of his life".[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-Williamson-21)

## Career
In 2009, Somerhalder appeared in the movie _The Tournament_ where he played the role of an assassin participating in a lethal competition with other assassins. He appears in the coffee table book _About Face_ by celebrity photographer John Russo.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-23) Also in 2009, Somerhalder began playing the role of Vampire Damon Salvatore as a series regular in The CW television drama series _The Vampire Diaries_. The series premiere attracted The CW's highest premiere ratings of any season premiere since the network began in 2006. The series has continued to be the highest-rated series on its channel with both his performance and the show receiving a positive response from critics. He began directing _The Vampire Diaries_ in its third season and produced the series at the start of season 8. He received several Teen Choice Awards and a [People's Choice Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Choice_Award "People's Choice Award") for his participation on the series.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-24)
Somerhalder acted in the short subject _Time Framed_ (2013).[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-25) He played Dr. Luther Swann as a series regular in the Netflixscience fictionhorror series _V Wars_, which ran from 2019 to 2020.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-26)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-28)

## Career
In 2020, Somerhalder shot footage for and served as an executive producer on the film _Kiss the Ground,_ a documentary centered on regenerative agriculture.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-29) He returned as an executive producer on its follow-up documentary, _Common Ground_, in 2023.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-30)
In a 2024 interview, Somerhalder revealed that he had retired from acting after relocating to a farm outside of Los Angeles, though he would still be involved in producing and environmental activism.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-31)

## Foundations and causes
Paul Wesley, Nina Dobrev and Somerhalder in 2012
Somerhalder was involved in the cleanup after the _Deepwater Horizon_ oil drilling disaster on April 22, 2010. His efforts included cleaning of oiled wildlife and taping public service announcements to let the public know how they could help.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-32) Somerhalder also supports the St. Tammany Humane Society, an organization for animal shelter and welfare. On November 13, 2010, he hosted a Bash on the Bayou charity fundraiser for the Society. During the event, Somerhalder was presented with a donation of $11,100 by _The Vampire Diaries_fandom for his birthday project.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-33)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-34)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-35)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-36)
Together with his _The Vampire Diaries_ co-stars Candice Accola and Michael Trevino, Somerhalder supports the It Gets Better Project, which makes it a goal to prevent suicide among LGBT youth[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-37) associated with The Trevor Project.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-38) For his second campaign, Somerhalder teamed up with _The Vampire Diaries_ co-star Paul Wesley to release a limited edition shirt designed by a fan, with the words "Blood Brothers Since 1864."[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-39) This campaign sold almost 10,000 shirts.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-40)

## Foundations and causes
On December 8, 2010, Somerhalder's 32nd birthday, he launched the "Ian Somerhalder Foundation" which he hopes will educate people on the importance of protecting the environment and animals: "Instead of gifts this year, my birthday wish is that we come together and raise funds to support projects that protect our habitat and nurture our furry friends."[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-41)[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-42) To spread awareness for his foundation, Somerhalder sponsors and often walks in Mardi Paws, a parade and organization held in his hometown of Covington.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-43) He opposes GMO foods and factory farming, and supports ecologistAllan Savory in his crusade to let cows graze in sync with nature to enrich soil, enhance biodiversity, and reverse climate change. In 2011, Somerhalder visited Savory in Africa and announced he was making a documentary about him with the goal of winning him a Nobel Prize.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-isfsavory-44)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-esavory-45)
Somerhalder is also a celebrity campaigner for RYOT, a Los Angeles-based media company known for RYOT.org, its cause-based, take action online news source.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-46)

## Personal life
Somerhalder dated his _Vampire Diaries_ co-star Nina Dobrev from 2010 to 2013.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-47) In 2014, he began dating actress Nikki Reed.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-48) They married on April 26, 2015, in Malibu, California.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-49) They had a daughter in 2017,[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-50)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-51) and a son in 2023.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-52)
While working on _Lost,_ Somerhalder and Maggie Grace adopted a feral cat named Roo which that they found "literally dying" in the jungle, and it later became Grace's "travel buddy."[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-53) Somerhalder stated that being a part of _Lost_ was "the greatest experience" of "the greatest year of his life".[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-54)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-55)

## Personal life
### Brother's Bond Bourbon
Somerhalder has remained close friends with his former _Vampire Diaries_ co-star Paul Wesley, and in 2020, they announced the launch of a straight bourbon whiskey named Brother's Bond Bourbon.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-56)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Somerhalder#cite_note-57)

Title: Ian Somerhalder Reveals ‘Controversial’ Reason He Left Hollywood and ‘Pulled the Plug’ on His Acting Career
Chunks: 0,1
### NEED TO KNOW
*   Ian Somerhalder stepped away from Hollywood in August 2019

*   In a new interview, he revealed the "really honest" reason behind his exit, which was a result of _V Wars_' cancellation

*   "I am not here for my career and livelihood to be dictated by someone who has mommy or daddy issues, or they weren't popular in school," he said
Nearly seven years after his exit, Ian Somerhalder is finally revealing the true reason he quit acting.
Somerhalder, 47, departed Hollywood in August 2019 and has since turned his focus to other business ventures with his wife, Nikki Reed, after they moved to a Calif. farm.
He shared the "really honest, kind of controversial" reason that he decided to pivot on the July 9 episode of the _Haley on the Go_ podcast, as he recalled how the cancellation of his Netflix series, _V Wars_, affected him.
"I wanted to do _V Wars_ because it was me, not as a vampire, it was me as a scientist," he said of the series. "[We] shot the show, moved my whole family to Northern Ontario. Worked really hard on this thing for almost a year, and the show that got turned in wasn't even watchable."
"I said to the studio, I don't want to put my name on this. I'll give you the money back — I'll give you millions of dollars. And they were like, 'What? What are you talking about?' "
_Ian Somerhalder in 'V Wars'_
_Credit: Netflix_
Somerhalder claimed he told Netflix that he and his producing partner, James Gibb, needed "creative control of the show" to fix it. "Netflix said, 'Sure. We're not giving you a dollar more.' "
He and Gibb raised more than $6 million to fix the series, Somerhalder said, and filmed "10 or 12 hours of footage in about six days," which landed him "in the hospital" from overworking his body.

### NEED TO KNOW
When the show premiered in December 2019, it was a "hit," Somerhalder said, but it was canceled anyway. Somerhalder alleged, "The execs were fighting, and someone quietly canceled the show. And the powers that be at Netflix were like, 'It's unfortunate. Yes, it shouldn't have happened. We can't go back, because it would set a precedent that would be terrible, so the show is done.' "
"I looked at myself in the mirror, and I said to my wife, I was like, man, I'm 40 years old. I don't want to spend two years of my life doing something, working this hard — one year fully unpaid — for this executive who had issues in high school, so they want to exert power now, [to cancel it]," Somerhalder said. "I am not here for my career and livelihood to be dictated by someone who has mommy or daddy issues, or they weren't popular in school."
"So I pulled the plug. That was it. I walked away," he said. "These executives are bitching at each other, and I'm like, are you kidding me? Done. I'm out."

_Nikki Reed and Ian Somerhalder at the EMA Awards Gala at Radford Studio Center on October 26, 2024_
_Credit: Gregg DeGuire/Getty_
There's a possibility, albeit slim, of Somerhalder making a return to Hollywood. In 2024, he told PEOPLE that acting is "in the rearview mirror," but also shared a more positive update.
"We got the rights back for _V Wars_," he revealed. "But I just don't know how the hell we would ever make a TV show."

**Nicholas Edward Cave** (born 22 September 1957[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-2)) is an Australian singer, musician and writer. He is the frontman of the rock band Nick Cave and the Bad Seeds. Known for his baritone voice, Cave's music is characterised by emotional intensity, a wide variety of influences and lyrical obsessions with death, religion, love, and violence.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-erlewine-3)

Born and raised in rural Victoria, Cave studied art in Melbourne before fronting The Birthday Party, one of the city's leading post-punk bands, in the late 1970s. In 1980, the band moved to London, England. Disillusioned by their stay there, they evolved towards a darker and more challenging sound that helped inspire gothic rock, and they acquired a reputation as "the most violent live band in the world".[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-4) Cave became recognised for his confrontational performances, his shock of black hair and pale, emaciated look. The band broke up soon after relocating to West Berlin in 1982. The following year, Cave formed Nick Cave and the Bad Seeds, later described as one of rock's "most redoubtable, enduring" bands.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-5) Much of their early material is set in a mythic American Deep South, drawing on spirituals and Delta blues, while Cave's preoccupation with Old Testament notions of good versus evil culminated in what has been called his signature song, "The Mercy Seat" (1988), and in his debut novel, _And the Ass Saw the Angel_ (1989). In 1988, he appeared in _Ghosts… of the Civil Dead_, an Australian prison film which he both co-wrote and scored.

The 1990s saw Cave move between São Paulo and England and found inspiration in the New Testament. He went on to achieve mainstream success with quieter, piano-driven ballads, notably the Kylie Minogue duet "Where the Wild Roses Grow" (1996), and "Into My Arms" (1997). Turning increasingly to film in the 2000s, Cave wrote the Australian Western _The Proposition_ (2005), also composing its soundtrack with frequent collaborator Warren Ellis. The pair's film score credits include _The Assassination of Jesse James by the Coward Robert Ford_ (2007), _The Road_ (2009) and _Hell or High Water_ (2016). Their garage rock side project Grinderman has released two studio albums since 2006. In 2009, he released his second novel, _The Death of Bunny Munro_, and starred in the semi-fictional "day in the life" film _20,000 Days on Earth_ (2014). His more recent musical work features ambient and electronic elements, as well as increasingly abstract lyrics, informed in part by grief over his son Arthur's 2015 death, which is explored in the documentary _One More Time with Feeling_ (2016) and the Bad Seeds' 2019 album _Ghosteen_. The band's 18th and latest album, _Wild God_, was released in 2024.
Since 2018, Cave has maintained _The Red Hand Files_, a newsletter he uses to respond to questions from fans. He has collaborated with the likes of Johnny Cash, Shane MacGowan and ex-partner PJ Harvey. His songs have also been covered by a wide range of artists, including Cash ("The Mercy Seat"), Metallica ("Loverman") and Snoop Dogg ("Red Right Hand"). He was inducted into the ARIA Hall of Fame in 2007,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-6) and he was named an Officer of the Order of Australia in 2017.

## Early life and education
[edit]
Cave was a choirboy at the Holy Trinity Cathedral in his hometown of Wangaratta.
Nicholas Edward Cave was born on 22 September 1957 in Warracknabeal, a country town in the Australian state of Victoria, to Dawn Cave (née Treadwell) and Colin Frank Cave.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-museum-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-8) He has two older brothers, Tim (born 1952) and Peter (born 1954), and a younger sister, Julie (born 1959).[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-9) As a child, he lived in Warracknabeal and then Wangaratta in rural Victoria.
His father taught English and mathematics at the local technical school; his mother was a librarian at the high school that Cave attended.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-oldnick-10) From an early age, Cave's father read him literary classics, such as _Crime and Punishment_ (1866) and _Lolita_ (1955),[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-devil-11) and also organised the first symposium on the Australian bushranger and outlaw Ned Kelly,[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-12) with whom Cave was enamoured as a child.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-dorian-13) Through his older brother, Cave became a fan of British progressive rock bands such as King Crimson, Pink Floyd and Jethro Tull,[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-14) while a childhood girlfriend introduced him to the Canadian folk artist Leonard Cohen, who he later described as "the greatest songwriter of them all".[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-15)

## Early life and education
When Cave was nine he joined the choir of Wangaratta's Holy Trinity Cathedral.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-museum-7) At 13 he was expelled from Wangaratta High School,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-devil-11) and sent by his parents to Melbourne to become a boarder and later day student at Caulfield Grammar School.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-oldnick-10) His family moved to Melbourne the following year, settling in the suburb of Murrumbeena. After his secondary schooling, Cave studied painting at the Caulfield Institute of Technology in 1976, but dropped out the following year to pursue music.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-Big-16) He also began using heroin around the time that he left art school.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-17)
Cave attended his first music concert at Melbourne's Festival Hall. The bill consisted of the English rock bands Manfred Mann, Deep Purple and Free. Cave recalled: "I remember sitting there and feeling physically the sound going through me."[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-Big-16) In early 1977, he saw the Australian punk rock bands Radio Birdman and the Saints live for the first time. Cave was particularly inspired by the show of the latter band, saying that he left the venue "a different person."[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-19)

## Early life and education
Cave was 19 when his father was killed in a car collision; his mother told him of his father's death while she was bailing him out of a St Kilda police station where he was being held on a charge of burglary.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-Bish-20) He would later recall that his father "died at a point in my life when I was most confused" and that "the loss of my father created in my life a vacuum, a space in which my words began to float and collect and find their purpose".[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-devil-11)

## Early life and education
### Early years and the Birthday Party (1973–1983)
[edit]
In 1973, Cave founded a band with fellow students at Caulfield Grammar. With Cave as lead vocalist, the band included Mick Harvey (guitar), Phill Calvert (drums), John Cochivera (guitar), Brett Purcell (bass guitar), and Chris Coyne (saxophone). Their repertoire consisted of cover versions of songs by Lou Reed, David Bowie, Alice Cooper, Roxy Music and Alex Harvey, among others. Later, the line-up slimmed down to four members including Cave's friend Tracy Pew on bass guitar. In 1977, after leaving school, they adopted the name the Boys Next Door and began playing predominantly original punk rock material. Guitarist, songwriter and ex-Young Charlatans member Rowland S. Howard joined the band in 1978.
The Melbourne post-punk venue the Crystal Ballroom, Cave's "first great stage"[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-walker-21)
The Boys Next Door emerged as the linchpin of the Melbourne post-punk scene in the late 1970s, securing a residency at St Kilda's Crystal Ballroom venue, where they attracted a cult following.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-walker-21) They played hundreds of live shows in Australia and toured interstate before changing their name to the Birthday Party in 1980 and moving to London, England. Cave's girlfriend and muse Anita Lane accompanied the band. They struggled initially with financial instability and limited connections, and grew to detest London and much of its music scene, which Cave later described as "dead, ... we felt really ripped off, robbed". He did however greatly admire the Pop Group,[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-22) and the Birthday Party shared a mutual affinity with the Fall.

## Early life and education
### Early years and the Birthday Party (1973–1983)
By the end of their first year in London, the Birthday Party had gained notoriety for their aggressive, confrontational live shows and Cave's unhinged stage presence, with him shrieking, bellowing and throwing himself about the stage, backed up by harsh pounding rock music laced with guitar feedback. Drawing on Old Testament imagery, Cave's lyrics frequently revolved around sin, debauchery and damnation.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-rey-23) The band found a champion in prominent radio DJ and taste-maker John Peel, and went on to record four Peel Sessions.
Cave's droll sense of humour and penchant for parody is evident in many of the band's songs, including "Nick the Stripper" and "King Ink". "Release the Bats", one of the band's most famous songs and John Peel's single of the year in 1981, was intended as an over-the-top "piss-take" on gothic rock, and a "direct attack" on the "stock gothic associations that less informed critics were wont to make". Ironically, it became highly influential on the genre, giving rise to a new generation of bands in England.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-24)
The Birthday Party relocated to West Berlin in 1982. After establishing a cult following in Europe, Australia and the United States, they disbanded in the following year.

## Early life and education
### Music in film and television
#### Film scores and theatre music
On 21 January 2008, a special edition of Cave's novel _And the Ass Saw the Angel_ was released.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-64) Cave's second novel _The Death of Bunny Munro_ was published on 8 September 2009 by HarperCollins.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-65)[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-66) Telling the story of a sex-addicted salesman, it was also released as a binaural audio-book produced by British Artists Iain Forsyth and Jane Pollard and an iPhone app.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-67) The book originally started as a screenplay Cave was going to write for John Hillcoat.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-68)
_The Death of Bunny Munro_ was made into a television series starring Matt Smith in 2025.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-69)
In 2015 he released the book _The Sick Bag Song_, followed in 2022 by _Faith, Hope, and Carnage_, collected from a series of phone conversations conducted between Cave and Irish writer [Sean O'Hagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_O'Hagan_(journalist) "Sean O'Hagan (journalist)") during the COVID-19 pandemic.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-70)

## Early life and education
### Music in film and television
#### Film scores and theatre music
Cave's writing has also attracted significant academic interest. Edited collections such as _Cultural Seeds: Essays on the Work of Nick Cave_ (2009) and _The Art of Nick Cave: New Critical Essays_ (2013) situate his lyrics and prose within literary and cultural studies. Scholars have emphasized his recurring biblical imagery, gothic motifs, and use of myth, with one contributor describing him as "a master of the disturbing narrative".[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-71)
Aside from their soundtracks, Cave also wrote the screenplays for John Hillcoat's _The Proposition_ (2005) and _Lawless_ (2012).
Cave wrote the foreword to a Canongate publication of the _Gospel According to Mark_, published in the UK in 1998. The American edition of the same book (published by Grove Press) contains a foreword by the noted American writer Barry Hannah.
Cave was a contributor to a biography of the alternative rock and pop band the Triffids, _Vagabond Holes: David McComb and the Triffids_ (2009), edited by Australian academics Niall Lucy and Chris Coughran.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-72)
Cave's first film appearance was in Wim Wenders' 1987 film _Wings of Desire_, in which he and the Bad Seeds are shown performing at a concert in Berlin.
Cave has made occasional appearances as an actor. He appears alongside Blixa Bargeld in the 1988 Peter Sempel film _Dandy_, playing dice, singing and speaking from his Berlin apartment. He is most prominently featured in the 1989 film _Ghosts… of the Civil Dead_, written and directed by John Hillcoat, and in the 1991 film _Johnny Suede_ with Brad Pitt.

## Early life and education
### Music in film and television
#### Film scores and theatre music
Cave appeared in the 2005 homage to Leonard Cohen, _[Leonard Cohen: I'm Your Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard\_Cohen:\_I'm\_Your\_Man "Leonard Cohen: I'm Your Man")_, in which he performed "[I'm Your Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I'm_Your_Man_(Leonard_Cohen_song) "I'm Your Man (Leonard Cohen song)")" solo, and "Suzanne" with Julie Christensen and Perla Batalla. He also appeared in the 2007 film adaptation of Ron Hansen's novel _The Assassination of Jesse James by the Coward Robert Ford_, where he sings "The Ballad of Jesse James".[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-73) Cave and Warren Ellis are credited for the film's soundtrack.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-74) Nick Cave and his son Luke performed one of the songs on the soundtrack together. Luke played the triangle.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-imdb.com-75)
His interest in the work of Edward Gorey led to his participation in the BBC Radio 3 programme _Guest + Host = Ghost_, featuring Peter Blegvad and the radiophonic sound of the Langham Research Centre.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-76)
Cave lent his voice in narrating the animated film _The Cat Piano_ (2009). It was directed by Eddie White and Ari Gibson (of [the People's Republic of Animation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_People's_Republic_of_Animation "The People's Republic of Animation")), produced by Jessica Brentnall and features music by Benjamin Speed.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-77)
He provided the voice of the character Bill Clarke in the stop-motion film _Memoir of a Snail_ (2024) by Adam Elliot.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-78)

## Early life and education
### Music in film and television
#### Film scores and theatre music
Cave at the 2012 Cannes Film Festival
Cave wrote the screenplay for _The Proposition_, a film about bushrangers in the Australian outback during the late 19th century. Directed by John Hillcoat and filmed in Queensland in 2004, it premiered in October 2005 and was later released worldwide to critical acclaim.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-79) Cave explained his personal background in relation to writing the film's screenplay in a 2013 interview:
> I had written long-form before but it is pure story-telling in script writing and that goes back as far as I can remember for me, not just with my father but with myself. I slept in the same bedroom as my sister for many years, until it became indecent to do so, and I would tell her stories every night—that is how she would get to sleep. She would say "tell me a story" so I would tell her a story. So that ability, I very much had that from the start and I used to enjoy that at school so actually to write a script—it suddenly felt like I was just making up a big story.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-Big-16)
The film critic for British newspaper _The Independent_ called _The Proposition_ "peerless", "a star-studded and uncompromisingly violent outlaw film".[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-80) The generally ambient soundtrack was recorded by Cave and Warren Ellis.
At the request of his friend Russell Crowe, Cave wrote a script for a proposed sequel to _Gladiator_ which was rejected by the studio.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-81)
An announcement in February 2010 stated that Andy Serkis and Cave would collaborate on a motion-capture movie of the Brecht and Weill musical _The Threepenny Opera_. As of November 2024, the project has not been realised.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-82)

## Early life and education
### Music in film and television
#### Film scores and theatre music
Cave wrote a screenplay titled _The Wettest County in the World_,[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-score-83) which was used for the 2012 film _Lawless_, directed again by John Hillcoat, starring Tom Hardy and Shia LaBeouf.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-84)
Cave currently maintains a personal blog and an online correspondence page with his fans called _The Red Hand Files_ which is seen as a continuation of _In Conversation,_ a series of live personal talks Cave had held in which the audience were free to ask questions. On the page, Cave discusses various issues ranging from art, religion, current affairs and music, as well as using it as a free platform in which fans are encouraged to ask personal questions on any topic of their choosing.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-Clarke-85)[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-Cunningham-86) Cave's intimate approach to the Question & Answer format on _The Red Hand Files_ was praised by _The Guardian_ as "a shelter from the online storm free of discord and conspiracies, and in harmony with the internet vision of Tim Berners-Lee."[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-Cunningham-86)

## Early life and education
### Music in film and television
#### Film scores and theatre music
In January 2023, after being sent a song written by ChatGPT "in the style of Nick Cave",[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-Guardian-2023-87) he responded on _The Red Hand Files_ (and was later quoted in _The Guardian_) saying that act of song writing "is not mimicry, or replication, or pastiche, it is the opposite, it is an act of self-murder that destroys all one has strived to produce in the past." He went on to say "It's a blood and guts business [that] requires my humanness", concluding that "this song is bullshit, a grotesque mockery of what it is to be human, and, well, I don't much like it."[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-Guardian-2023-87)[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-88)

## Legacy and influence
[edit]
In 2010, Cave was ranked the 19th greatest living lyricist in _NME_.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-89)Flea of the Red Hot Chili Peppers called him the greatest living songwriter in 2011.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-90) Rob O'Connor of Yahoo Music listed him as the 23rd best lyricist in rock history.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-91)_The Art of Nick Cave: New Critical Essays_ was edited by academic John H. Baker and published in 2013. In an essay on the studio album _[The Boatman's Call](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Boatman's\_Call "The Boatman's Call")_ (1997), Peter Billingham praised Cave's love songs as characterised by a "deep, poetic, melancholic introspection".[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBaker201313-92) Carl Lavery, another academic featured in the collection, argued that there was a "burgeoning field of Cave studies".[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBaker201329-93) Dan Rose argued that Cave "is a master of the disturbing narrative and chronicler of the extreme, though he is also certainly capable of a subtle romantic vision. He does much to the listener who enters his world."[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBaker201398-94)

## Legacy and influence
Songs written about Cave include "Just a King in Mirrors" (1983) by the Go-Betweens,[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-95) "Sick Man" (1984) by Foetus,[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-96) and "Bill Bailey" (1987) by the Gun Club.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-97)
A number of prominent noise rock vocalists have cited Cave's Birthday Party-era work as their primary influence, including the U-Men's John Bigley,[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-98) and David Yow, frontman of Scratch Acid and the Jesus Lizard. Yow stated: "For a long time, particularly with Scratch Acid, I was so taken with the Birthday Party that I would deny it",[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-99) and that "it sounded like I was trying to be Birthday Party Nick Cave—which I was."[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-100) Often compared to Cave in his vocal delivery, Alexis Marshall of Daughters said that he admires the personality and energy within Cave's voice, and that his early studio albums "exposed [him] to lyrical content as literature".[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-101)
Due to his contributions to the world of culture and art, Nick Cave was awarded the insignia of Knight of the Order of Arts and Letters of France in 2025.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-102)

**Nicholas Edward Cave** (born 22 September 1957[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-2)) is an Australian singer, musician and writer. He is the frontman of the rock band Nick Cave and the Bad Seeds. Known for his baritone voice, Cave's music is characterised by emotional intensity, a wide variety of influences and lyrical obsessions with death, religion, love, and violence.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-erlewine-3)
texts.1: Born and raised in rural Victoria, Cave studied art in Melbourne before fronting The Birthday Party, one of the city's leading post-punk bands, in the late 1970s. In 1980, the band moved to London, England. Disillusioned by their stay there, they evolved towards a darker and more challenging sound that helped inspire gothic rock, and they acquired a reputation as "the most violent live band in the world".[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-4) Cave became recognised for his confrontational performances, his shock of black hair and pale, emaciated look. The band broke up soon after relocating to West Berlin in 1982. The following year, Cave formed Nick Cave and the Bad Seeds, later described as one of rock's "most redoubtable, enduring" bands.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-5) Much of their early material is set in a mythic American Deep South, drawing on spirituals and Delta blues, while Cave's preoccupation with Old Testament notions of good versus evil culminated in what has been called his signature song, "The Mercy Seat" (1988), and in his debut novel, _And the Ass Saw the Angel_ (1989). In 1988, he appeared in _Ghosts… of the Civil Dead_, an Australian prison film which he both co-wrote and scored.
texts.2:
The 1990s saw Cave move between São Paulo and England and found inspiration in the New Testament. He went on to achieve mainstream success with quieter, piano-driven ballads, notably the Kylie Minogue duet "Where the Wild Roses Grow" (1996), and "Into My Arms" (1997). Turning increasingly to film in the 2000s, Cave wrote the Australian Western _The Proposition_ (2005), also composing its soundtrack with frequent collaborator Warren Ellis. The pair's film score credits include _The Assassination of Jesse James by the Coward Robert Ford_ (2007), _The Road_ (2009) and _Hell or High Water_ (2016). Their garage rock side project Grinderman has released two studio albums since 2006. In 2009, he released his second novel, _The Death of Bunny Munro_, and starred in the semi-fictional "day in the life" film _20,000 Days on Earth_ (2014). His more recent musical work features ambient and electronic elements, as well as increasingly abstract lyrics, informed in part by grief over his son Arthur's 2015 death, which is explored in the documentary _One More Time with Feeling_ (2016) and the Bad Seeds' 2019 album _Ghosteen_. The band's 18th and latest album, _Wild God_, was released in 2024.
Since 2018, Cave has maintained _The Red Hand Files_, a newsletter he uses to respond to questions from fans. He has collaborated with the likes of Johnny Cash, Shane MacGowan and ex-partner PJ Harvey. His songs have also been covered by a wide range of artists, including Cash ("The Mercy Seat"), Metallica ("Loverman") and Snoop Dogg ("Red Right Hand"). He was inducted into the ARIA Hall of Fame in 2007,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-6) and he was named an Officer of the Order of Australia in 2017.

## Early life and education
[edit]
Cave was a choirboy at the Holy Trinity Cathedral in his hometown of Wangaratta.
Nicholas Edward Cave was born on 22 September 1957 in Warracknabeal, a country town in the Australian state of Victoria, to Dawn Cave (née Treadwell) and Colin Frank Cave.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-museum-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-8) He has two older brothers, Tim (born 1952) and Peter (born 1954), and a younger sister, Julie (born 1959).[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-9) As a child, he lived in Warracknabeal and then Wangaratta in rural Victoria.
His father taught English and mathematics at the local technical school; his mother was a librarian at the high school that Cave attended.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-oldnick-10) From an early age, Cave's father read him literary classics, such as _Crime and Punishment_ (1866) and _Lolita_ (1955),[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-devil-11) and also organised the first symposium on the Australian bushranger and outlaw Ned Kelly,[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-12) with whom Cave was enamoured as a child.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-dorian-13) Through his older brother, Cave became a fan of British progressive rock bands such as King Crimson, Pink Floyd and Jethro Tull,[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-14) while a childhood girlfriend introduced him to the Canadian folk artist Leonard Cohen, who he later described as "the greatest songwriter of them all".[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-15)

## Early life and education
When Cave was nine he joined the choir of Wangaratta's Holy Trinity Cathedral.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-museum-7) At 13 he was expelled from Wangaratta High School,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-devil-11) and sent by his parents to Melbourne to become a boarder and later day student at Caulfield Grammar School.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-oldnick-10) His family moved to Melbourne the following year, settling in the suburb of Murrumbeena. After his secondary schooling, Cave studied painting at the Caulfield Institute of Technology in 1976, but dropped out the following year to pursue music.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-Big-16) He also began using heroin around the time that he left art school.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-17)
Cave attended his first music concert at Melbourne's Festival Hall. The bill consisted of the English rock bands Manfred Mann, Deep Purple and Free. Cave recalled: "I remember sitting there and feeling physically the sound going through me."[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-Big-16) In early 1977, he saw the Australian punk rock bands Radio Birdman and the Saints live for the first time. Cave was particularly inspired by the show of the latter band, saying that he left the venue "a different person."[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-19)

## Early life and education
Cave was 19 when his father was killed in a car collision; his mother told him of his father's death while she was bailing him out of a St Kilda police station where he was being held on a charge of burglary.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-Bish-20) He would later recall that his father "died at a point in my life when I was most confused" and that "the loss of my father created in my life a vacuum, a space in which my words began to float and collect and find their purpose".[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-devil-11)

Cave at the 2012 Cannes Film Festival
Cave wrote the screenplay for _The Proposition_, a film about bushrangers in the Australian outback during the late 19th century. Directed by John Hillcoat and filmed in Queensland in 2004, it premiered in October 2005 and was later released worldwide to critical acclaim.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-79) Cave explained his personal background in relation to writing the film's screenplay in a 2013 interview:
> I had written long-form before but it is pure story-telling in script writing and that goes back as far as I can remember for me, not just with my father but with myself. I slept in the same bedroom as my sister for many years, until it became indecent to do so, and I would tell her stories every night—that is how she would get to sleep. She would say "tell me a story" so I would tell her a story. So that ability, I very much had that from the start and I used to enjoy that at school so actually to write a script—it suddenly felt like I was just making up a big story.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-Big-16)
The film critic for British newspaper _The Independent_ called _The Proposition_ "peerless", "a star-studded and uncompromisingly violent outlaw film".[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-80) The generally ambient soundtrack was recorded by Cave and Warren Ellis.
At the request of his friend Russell Crowe, Cave wrote a script for a proposed sequel to _Gladiator_ which was rejected by the studio.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-81)
An announcement in February 2010 stated that Andy Serkis and Cave would collaborate on a motion-capture movie of the Brecht and Weill musical _The Threepenny Opera_. As of November 2024, the project has not been realised.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-82)

On the page, Cave discusses various issues ranging from art, religion, current affairs and music, as well as using it as a free platform in which fans are encouraged to ask personal questions on any topic of their choosing.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-Clarke-85)[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-Cunningham-86) Cave's intimate approach to the Question & Answer format on _The Red Hand Files_ was praised by _The Guardian_ as "a shelter from the online storm free of discord and conspiracies, and in harmony with the internet vision of Tim Berners-Lee."[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-Cunningham-86)

Baker and published in 2013. In an essay on the studio album _[The Boatman's Call](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Boatman's\_Call "The Boatman's Call")_ (1997), Peter Billingham praised Cave's love songs as characterised by a "deep, poetic, melancholic introspection".[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBaker201313-92) Carl Lavery, another academic featured in the collection, argued that there was a "burgeoning field of Cave studies".[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBaker201329-93) Dan Rose argued that Cave "is a master of the disturbing narrative and chronicler of the extreme, though he is also certainly capable of a subtle romantic vision. ## Legacy and influence
Songs written about Cave include "Just a King in Mirrors" (1983) by the Go-Betweens,[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-95) "Sick Man" (1984) by Foetus,[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-96) and "Bill Bailey" (1987) by the Gun Club.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-97)
A number of prominent noise rock vocalists have cited Cave's Birthday Party-era work as their primary influence, including the U-Men's John Bigley,[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-98) and David Yow, frontman of Scratch Acid and the Jesus Lizard. Yow stated: "For a long time, particularly with Scratch Acid, I was so taken with the Birthday Party that I would deny it",[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-99) and that "it sounded like I was trying to be Birthday Party Nick Cave—which I was."[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-100) Often compared to Cave in his vocal delivery, Alexis Marshall of Daughters said that he admires the personality and energy within Cave's voice, and that his early studio albums "exposed [him] to lyrical content as literature".[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-101)
Due to his contributions to the world of culture and art, Nick Cave was awarded the insignia of Knight of the Order of Arts and Letters of France in 2025.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-102)

**Nicholas Edward Cave** (born 22 September 1957[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-2)) is an Australian singer, musician and writer. He is the frontman of the rock band Nick Cave and the Bad Seeds. Known for his baritone voice, Cave's music is characterised by emotional intensity, a wide variety of influences and lyrical obsessions with death, religion, love, and violence.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-erlewine-3)

Born and raised in rural Victoria, Cave studied art in Melbourne before fronting The Birthday Party, one of the city's leading post-punk bands, in the late 1970s. In 1980, the band moved to London, England. Disillusioned by their stay there, they evolved towards a darker and more challenging sound that helped inspire gothic rock, and they acquired a reputation as "the most violent live band in the world".[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-4) Cave became recognised for his confrontational performances, his shock of black hair and pale, emaciated look. The band broke up soon after relocating to West Berlin in 1982. The following year, Cave formed Nick Cave and the Bad Seeds, later described as one of rock's "most redoubtable, enduring" bands.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-5) Much of their early material is set in a mythic American Deep South, drawing on spirituals and Delta blues, while Cave's preoccupation with Old Testament notions of good versus evil culminated in what has been called his signature song, "The Mercy Seat" (1988), and in his debut novel, _And the Ass Saw the Angel_ (1989). In 1988, he appeared in _Ghosts… of the Civil Dead_, an Australian prison film which he both co-wrote and scored.

The 1990s saw Cave move between São Paulo and England and found inspiration in the New Testament. He went on to achieve mainstream success with quieter, piano-driven ballads, notably the Kylie Minogue duet "Where the Wild Roses Grow" (1996), and "Into My Arms" (1997). Turning increasingly to film in the 2000s, Cave wrote the Australian Western _The Proposition_ (2005), also composing its soundtrack with frequent collaborator Warren Ellis. The pair's film score credits include _The Assassination of Jesse James by the Coward Robert Ford_ (2007), _The Road_ (2009) and _Hell or High Water_ (2016). Their garage rock side project Grinderman has released two studio albums since 2006. In 2009, he released his second novel, _The Death of Bunny Munro_, and starred in the semi-fictional "day in the life" film _20,000 Days on Earth_ (2014). His more recent musical work features ambient and electronic elements, as well as increasingly abstract lyrics, informed in part by grief over his son Arthur's 2015 death, which is explored in the documentary _One More Time with Feeling_ (2016) and the Bad Seeds' 2019 album _Ghosteen_. The band's 18th and latest album, _Wild God_, was released in 2024.
Since 2018, Cave has maintained _The Red Hand Files_, a newsletter he uses to respond to questions from fans. He has collaborated with the likes of Johnny Cash, Shane MacGowan and ex-partner PJ Harvey. His songs have also been covered by a wide range of artists, including Cash ("The Mercy Seat"), Metallica ("Loverman") and Snoop Dogg ("Red Right Hand"). He was inducted into the ARIA Hall of Fame in 2007,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-6) and he was named an Officer of the Order of Australia in 2017.

## Early life and education
[edit]
Cave was a choirboy at the Holy Trinity Cathedral in his hometown of Wangaratta.
Nicholas Edward Cave was born on 22 September 1957 in Warracknabeal, a country town in the Australian state of Victoria, to Dawn Cave (née Treadwell) and Colin Frank Cave.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-museum-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-8) He has two older brothers, Tim (born 1952) and Peter (born 1954), and a younger sister, Julie (born 1959).[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-9) As a child, he lived in Warracknabeal and then Wangaratta in rural Victoria.
His father taught English and mathematics at the local technical school; his mother was a librarian at the high school that Cave attended.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-oldnick-10) From an early age, Cave's father read him literary classics, such as _Crime and Punishment_ (1866) and _Lolita_ (1955),[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-devil-11) and also organised the first symposium on the Australian bushranger and outlaw Ned Kelly,[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-12) with whom Cave was enamoured as a child.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-dorian-13) Through his older brother, Cave became a fan of British progressive rock bands such as King Crimson, Pink Floyd and Jethro Tull,[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-14) while a childhood girlfriend introduced him to the Canadian folk artist Leonard Cohen, who he later described as "the greatest songwriter of them all".[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-15)

## Early life and education
When Cave was nine he joined the choir of Wangaratta's Holy Trinity Cathedral.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-museum-7) At 13 he was expelled from Wangaratta High School,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-devil-11) and sent by his parents to Melbourne to become a boarder and later day student at Caulfield Grammar School.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-oldnick-10) His family moved to Melbourne the following year, settling in the suburb of Murrumbeena. After his secondary schooling, Cave studied painting at the Caulfield Institute of Technology in 1976, but dropped out the following year to pursue music.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-Big-16) He also began using heroin around the time that he left art school.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-17)
Cave attended his first music concert at Melbourne's Festival Hall. The bill consisted of the English rock bands Manfred Mann, Deep Purple and Free. Cave recalled: "I remember sitting there and feeling physically the sound going through me."[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-Big-16) In early 1977, he saw the Australian punk rock bands Radio Birdman and the Saints live for the first time. Cave was particularly inspired by the show of the latter band, saying that he left the venue "a different person."[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-19)

## Early life and education
Cave was 19 when his father was killed in a car collision; his mother told him of his father's death while she was bailing him out of a St Kilda police station where he was being held on a charge of burglary.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-Bish-20) He would later recall that his father "died at a point in my life when I was most confused" and that "the loss of my father created in my life a vacuum, a space in which my words began to float and collect and find their purpose".[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-devil-11)

## Early life and education
### Early years and the Birthday Party (1973–1983)
[edit]
In 1973, Cave founded a band with fellow students at Caulfield Grammar. With Cave as lead vocalist, the band included Mick Harvey (guitar), Phill Calvert (drums), John Cochivera (guitar), Brett Purcell (bass guitar), and Chris Coyne (saxophone). Their repertoire consisted of cover versions of songs by Lou Reed, David Bowie, Alice Cooper, Roxy Music and Alex Harvey, among others. Later, the line-up slimmed down to four members including Cave's friend Tracy Pew on bass guitar. In 1977, after leaving school, they adopted the name the Boys Next Door and began playing predominantly original punk rock material. Guitarist, songwriter and ex-Young Charlatans member Rowland S. Howard joined the band in 1978.
The Melbourne post-punk venue the Crystal Ballroom, Cave's "first great stage"[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-walker-21)
The Boys Next Door emerged as the linchpin of the Melbourne post-punk scene in the late 1970s, securing a residency at St Kilda's Crystal Ballroom venue, where they attracted a cult following.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-walker-21) They played hundreds of live shows in Australia and toured interstate before changing their name to the Birthday Party in 1980 and moving to London, England. Cave's girlfriend and muse Anita Lane accompanied the band. They struggled initially with financial instability and limited connections, and grew to detest London and much of its music scene, which Cave later described as "dead, ... we felt really ripped off, robbed". He did however greatly admire the Pop Group,[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-22) and the Birthday Party shared a mutual affinity with the Fall.

## Early life and education
### Early years and the Birthday Party (1973–1983)
By the end of their first year in London, the Birthday Party had gained notoriety for their aggressive, confrontational live shows and Cave's unhinged stage presence, with him shrieking, bellowing and throwing himself about the stage, backed up by harsh pounding rock music laced with guitar feedback. Drawing on Old Testament imagery, Cave's lyrics frequently revolved around sin, debauchery and damnation.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-rey-23) The band found a champion in prominent radio DJ and taste-maker John Peel, and went on to record four Peel Sessions.
Cave's droll sense of humour and penchant for parody is evident in many of the band's songs, including "Nick the Stripper" and "King Ink". "Release the Bats", one of the band's most famous songs and John Peel's single of the year in 1981, was intended as an over-the-top "piss-take" on gothic rock, and a "direct attack" on the "stock gothic associations that less informed critics were wont to make". Ironically, it became highly influential on the genre, giving rise to a new generation of bands in England.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-24)
The Birthday Party relocated to West Berlin in 1982. After establishing a cult following in Europe, Australia and the United States, they disbanded in the following year.

#### Film scores and theatre music
On 21 January 2008, a special edition of Cave's novel _And the Ass Saw the Angel_ was released.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-64) Cave's second novel _The Death of Bunny Munro_ was published on 8 September 2009 by HarperCollins.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-65)[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-66) Telling the story of a sex-addicted salesman, it was also released as a binaural audio-book produced by British Artists Iain Forsyth and Jane Pollard and an iPhone app.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-67) The book originally started as a screenplay Cave was going to write for John Hillcoat.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-68)

Cave at the 2012 Cannes Film Festival
Cave wrote the screenplay for _The Proposition_, a film about bushrangers in the Australian outback during the late 19th century. Directed by John Hillcoat and filmed in Queensland in 2004, it premiered in October 2005 and was later released worldwide to critical acclaim.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-79) Cave explained his personal background in relation to writing the film's screenplay in a 2013 interview:
> I had written long-form before but it is pure story-telling in script writing and that goes back as far as I can remember for me, not just with my father but with myself. I slept in the same bedroom as my sister for many years, until it became indecent to do so, and I would tell her stories every night—that is how she would get to sleep. She would say "tell me a story" so I would tell her a story. So that ability, I very much had that from the start and I used to enjoy that at school so actually to write a script—it suddenly felt like I was just making up a big story.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-Big-16)
The film critic for British newspaper _The Independent_ called _The Proposition_ "peerless", "a star-studded and uncompromisingly violent outlaw film".[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-80) The generally ambient soundtrack was recorded by Cave and Warren Ellis.
At the request of his friend Russell Crowe, Cave wrote a script for a proposed sequel to _Gladiator_ which was rejected by the studio.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-81)
An announcement in February 2010 stated that Andy Serkis and Cave would collaborate on a motion-capture movie of the Brecht and Weill musical _The Threepenny Opera_. As of November 2024, the project has not been realised.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-82)

## Early life and education
### Music in film and television
#### Film scores and theatre music
Cave wrote a screenplay titled _The Wettest County in the World_,[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-score-83) which was used for the 2012 film _Lawless_, directed again by John Hillcoat, starring Tom Hardy and Shia LaBeouf.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-84)
Cave currently maintains a personal blog and an online correspondence page with his fans called _The Red Hand Files_ which is seen as a continuation of _In Conversation,_ a series of live personal talks Cave had held in which the audience were free to ask questions. On the page, Cave discusses various issues ranging from art, religion, current affairs and music, as well as using it as a free platform in which fans are encouraged to ask personal questions on any topic of their choosing.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-Clarke-85)[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-Cunningham-86) Cave's intimate approach to the Question & Answer format on _The Red Hand Files_ was praised by _The Guardian_ as "a shelter from the online storm free of discord and conspiracies, and in harmony with the internet vision of Tim Berners-Lee."[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-Cunningham-86)

## Early life and education
### Music in film and television
#### Film scores and theatre music
In January 2023, after being sent a song written by ChatGPT "in the style of Nick Cave",[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-Guardian-2023-87) he responded on _The Red Hand Files_ (and was later quoted in _The Guardian_) saying that act of song writing "is not mimicry, or replication, or pastiche, it is the opposite, it is an act of self-murder that destroys all one has strived to produce in the past." He went on to say "It's a blood and guts business [that] requires my humanness", concluding that "this song is bullshit, a grotesque mockery of what it is to be human, and, well, I don't much like it."[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-Guardian-2023-87)[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-88)

## Legacy and influence
[edit]
In 2010, Cave was ranked the 19th greatest living lyricist in _NME_.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-89)Flea of the Red Hot Chili Peppers called him the greatest living songwriter in 2011.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-90) Rob O'Connor of Yahoo Music listed him as the 23rd best lyricist in rock history.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-91)_The Art of Nick Cave: New Critical Essays_ was edited by academic John H. Baker and published in 2013. In an essay on the studio album _[The Boatman's Call](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Boatman's\_Call "The Boatman's Call")_ (1997), Peter Billingham praised Cave's love songs as characterised by a "deep, poetic, melancholic introspection".[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBaker201313-92) Carl Lavery, another academic featured in the collection, argued that there was a "burgeoning field of Cave studies".[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBaker201329-93) Dan Rose argued that Cave "is a master of the disturbing narrative and chronicler of the extreme, though he is also certainly capable of a subtle romantic vision. He does much to the listener who enters his world."[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBaker201398-94)

## Legacy and influence
Songs written about Cave include "Just a King in Mirrors" (1983) by the Go-Betweens,[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-95) "Sick Man" (1984) by Foetus,[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-96) and "Bill Bailey" (1987) by the Gun Club.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-97)
A number of prominent noise rock vocalists have cited Cave's Birthday Party-era work as their primary influence, including the U-Men's John Bigley,[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-98) and David Yow, frontman of Scratch Acid and the Jesus Lizard. Yow stated: "For a long time, particularly with Scratch Acid, I was so taken with the Birthday Party that I would deny it",[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-99) and that "it sounded like I was trying to be Birthday Party Nick Cave—which I was."[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-100) Often compared to Cave in his vocal delivery, Alexis Marshall of Daughters said that he admires the personality and energy within Cave's voice, and that his early studio albums "exposed [him] to lyrical content as literature".[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-101)
Due to his contributions to the world of culture and art, Nick Cave was awarded the insignia of Knight of the Order of Arts and Letters of France in 2025.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave#cite_note-102)

And when the world tells you to be practical, your dream just grins, flips its scarf, and says, “Places, please!” Auditions come and go like weather. Roles slip by like fireflies. But the magic—the real magic—lives in the moments you stand in a bare room, heart thrumming like an overture, and dare to become someone new. It lives in every script smudged with notes, in every midnight monologue, in every breath you take before stepping into the light. Don’t give up. You are built of spotlight and stubbornness, of imagination and grit. Somewhere, a director is waiting for you. Somewhere, an audience is waiting to feel something because of you.
